items.title: EER — Equal Error Rate
items.inshort: EER is the point where a biometric system wrongly accepts impostors exactly as often as it wrongly rejects genuine users. One number to compare verifiers; lower is better.

slides.title: Think of it like…
slides.text: A bouncer with a strictness dial: too strict and friends are turned away, too loose and strangers walk in. EER is the dial setting where both mistakes happen equally often.

slides.title: What it is
slides.text: FAR (false accept rate) falls and FRR (false reject rate) rises as you raise the threshold. EER is where the two curves cross.

slides.title: How it works
flow: Score every genuine and impostor pair
Compute FAR and FRR at each threshold

slides.title: The one formula
slides.text: EER = FAR(τ*) = FRR(τ*), where τ* is the threshold where the two rates meet.

slides.title: Common pitfalls
points: EER hides behaviour at the operating point you actually deploy (e.g. FAR=0.1%)
Small test sets make EER noisy — report confidence intervals

items.title: Grad-CAM — where is the model looking?
items.inshort: Grad-CAM makes a heatmap of the image regions that pushed a CNN toward its decision, using gradients of the class score w.r.t. the last conv features.

slides.title: Think of it like…
slides.text: Like asking a judge which parts of the evidence moved them most, and highlighting those pages.

slides.title: What it is
slides.text: It weights each feature map of a conv layer by how much the class score changes with it, sums them, and keeps the positive part.

slides.title: How it works
flow: Forward pass, pick a class score
Backprop to the last conv layer
Weighted sum of feature maps → ReLU → upsample

slides.title: The one formula
slides.text: L = ReLU( Σ_k α_k A^k ),  α_k = mean over pixels of ∂y_c/∂A^k  (A^k: k-th feature map, y_c: class score)

slides.title: Common pitfalls
points: Low resolution (size of the conv map)
A plausible heatmap does not prove the model is right

items.title: Vision Transformer in 5 slides
items.inshort: A ViT cuts an image into patches, turns each into a token, and lets every patch 'talk' to every other with self-attention — no convolutions needed.

slides.title: Think of it like…
slides.text: Tear a photo into stamps, label each stamp, and let a room full of people (patches) chat to decide what the whole photo shows.

slides.title: What it is
slides.text: Patches are linearly embedded, a position embedding is added, and a stack of Transformer encoder blocks processes the sequence. A [CLS] token gathers the global answer.

slides.title: How it works
flow: Add position embeddings and a [CLS] token

slides.title: The one formula
slides.text: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d) V — each token mixes information from all tokens, weighted by similarity.

slides.title: Common pitfalls
points: Cost grows with the square of the number of patches

items.title: Diffusion models without the maths fear
items.inshort: A diffusion model learns to remove noise step by step. Start from pure noise, denoise many times, and an image appears.

slides.title: Think of it like…
slides.text: Sculpting: start with a rough block (noise) and chip away a little at a time until the statue (image) emerges.

slides.title: What it is
slides.text: Training adds known noise to real images and teaches a network to predict that noise. Generation runs the process backwards.

slides.title: How it works
flow: Add Gaussian noise at a random level t → x_t
Network predicts the added noise ε
At sampling: start from noise, subtract predicted noise repeatedly
Latent diffusion does this in a compressed VAE space

slides.title: The one formula
slides.text: Loss = ‖ε − ε_θ(x_t, t)‖² — predict the noise ε that was added at step t.

slides.title: Common pitfalls
points: Reconstruction error is a tempting but brittle fake detector

items.title: Contrastive learning & CLIP
items.inshort: Contrastive learning pulls matching pairs together in embedding space and pushes non-matching pairs apart. CLIP does this with images and their captions.

slides.title: Think of it like…
slides.text: A party game: find your partner in a crowd. You get rewarded for standing next to your partner and far from everyone else.

slides.title: What it is
slides.text: For a batch of N pairs, the model scores all N×N combinations and trains so the true pairs win, using a softmax over similarities.

slides.title: The one formula
slides.text: ℓ_i = −log( exp(sim(i,i)/τ) / Σ_j exp(sim(i,j)/τ) ),  τ = temperature

items.title: Prototype networks — 'this looks like that'
items.inshort: Prototype models classify by comparing parts of an input to learned prototypical parts, so each decision can be explained by pointing at examples.

slides.title: Think of it like…
slides.text: A bird-watcher saying: 'it's a cardinal because this beak looks like that beak I've seen before.'

slides.title: What it is
slides.text: The network learns a set of prototype vectors per class. Each image patch is compared with each prototype; similarities feed a linear layer.

slides.title: How it works
flow: Project prototypes onto real training patches for visualization

slides.title: The one formula
slides.text: sim(z, p) = log( (‖z−p‖² + 1) / (‖z−p‖² + ε) )

items.title: JND — Just Noticeable Difference
items.inshort: JND is the smallest change a human can notice at each pixel. Watermarks hide more energy where JND is high (texture) and less where it is low (flat sky).

slides.title: Think of it like…
slides.text: Whispering in a noisy café vs. a silent library: you can say more in the café without anyone noticing.

slides.title: What it is
slides.text: A JND map estimates per-pixel visibility thresholds from luminance and texture masking. Scaling the watermark by this map keeps it invisible but strong.

slides.title: How it works
flow: Scale the watermark residual by the map

slides.title: The one formula
slides.text: x_w = x + α · JND(x) ⊙ r   (r: watermark residual, α: strength)

slides.title: Common pitfalls
points: Simple JND models ignore colour and viewing distance
Attackers can also exploit high-JND regions

items.title: Presentation Attack Detection (PAD)
items.inshort: PAD decides whether the thing in front of a biometric sensor is a live person or a spoof — a printed photo, a replayed video, a mask, or a synthetic voice.

slides.title: Think of it like…
slides.text: A cashier checking not just the photo on your ID, but that you are a real person and not a cardboard cut-out.

slides.title: What it is
slides.text: PAD models look for cues like texture, depth, reflection, micro-motion or spectral artifacts, and are evaluated with APCER and BPCER.

slides.title: How it works
flow: Extract liveness cues (texture, depth, rPPG, spectrum)
Report APCER (attacks accepted) and BPCER (real users rejected)

slides.title: The one formula
slides.text: APCER = attacks classified as bona fide / all attacks;  BPCER = bona fide classified as attacks / all bona fide

slides.title: Common pitfalls
points: Unseen attack types break most models
Deepfake injection attacks bypass the camera entirely
